utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good morning. Will the Registrar call the next case on the list, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-94-1-A, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The accused, or the appellant, shall we say, is present. Mr. Tadic signals his presence. May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I appear for the Prosecutor as appeals counsel with Brenda Hollis, senior trial attorney, and Michael Keegan, trial attorney, and assisted by Ann Sutherland, legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Your Honours, I appear on behalf of the appellant, Mr. John Livingston, assisted by Ms. Navaz Daruwalla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I say a few things? We are hoping, in the usual way, to have the coffee break at 11.15. We have read the documentation before us, and that suffices to signal our interest inasmuch as brevity conformable with comprehensiveness as may be possible. So I turn now to the scheduling order of 8th December, 1998, which forms the basis of our meeting this morning. I turn to operative paragraph 4 of that order in which the Appeals Chamber directed that oral arguments on such application for leave to amend shall, if needed, be heard on Monday, 25 January, 1999, commencing at 10.00, to be followed by a closed session Status Conference. The application for leave to amend, being that which is referred to in operative paragraph 2, in which the Appeals Chamber directed the appellant to file any application for leave to amend the notice of appeal and appellant's brief by Friday, 8 January, 1999. Now, counsel will move in support of the application. May I, as a matter of housekeeping, inquire how long counsel expects to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I was tempted to reply "as long as a piece of string," but I shall hope to take on board what Your Honour has said about the desirability for brevity in these proceedings, and I would hope to be able to complete my remarks, if not by the coffee break, certainly shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We have a kind of procrastinatory problem arising this way, that it turns out, because of other judicial commitments of other members of the Appeals Chamber, we will only have available to us this morning for the purposes of an inquiry into the particular matter which is before us. So perhaps you could bear that in mind? If, by any chance, it were possible for you to finish before the coffee break so that the other side could commence their response, that might facilitate the conclusion of the presentation in the course of this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I will do my best. I think there will come a point during the course of the morning when the Court perhaps ought to move into closed session because in order to address the Court as to the question of leave in relation to the second ground of appeal in the amended notice, that will touch upon matters that I would submit ought to be determined in closed session rather than in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What leave are you referring to, Mr. Clegg? Perhaps it is a good moment to invite you to address the objection made by the Prosecution, which you would have seen. The objection is to this effect, that the scheduling order made by this Court on 8th December, 1998, visualised that the appellant would be applying today for leave to file an amendment to its grounds of appeal, and what the Prosecution is saying is that they see no such motion for leave to file an amendment to the grounds of appeal, and consequently, I would suppose it would be their submission that there is nothing to activate the Court this morning, unless you are pleased to invite the Court to regard your amended notice of appeal as a de facto application for leave to amend.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I am grateful for that indication, and I can encourage the Court that I certainly will not take until the coffee break to deal with that part of the proceedings, and I can see no reason for the Court going into closed session in relation to that. The Court has already identified that the scheduling order in order number 4 identified today as the day for oral argument on an application for leave to amend. The Court, when it vacated the last date, was aware, by reason of the motion filed on behalf of the Defendant on page 5, that application was to be made to amend the appellant's notice of appeal and the appellant's brief, and it was in the light of that notice being given by the appellant that, firstly, the Prosecution did not object to the vacation of the last date, for which I am grateful, and secondly, that the Court itself vacated the last date and made the various orders identified already by the Court. The Court will be aware that I have only recently been instructed to appear on behalf of the appellant, and my first task, having familiarised myself with the facts of the case, was to consider the grounds of appeal drafted by each side and the briefs that accompanied them. It was that study that convinced me that some of the grounds of appeal settled by the appellant were unarguable and others were expressed in all-embracing language which didn't appear to focus on particular aspects of the appeal that I thought ought to be addressed. In my judgment, the appeal ought to have been expressed in rather more discrete terms, and one other ground hitherto not pleaded appeared ought to be the subject of an application for leave before this Chamber. It was against that background that I resolved to make an oral application for leave to amend the grounds of appeal today, the Court being aware of that intention by reason of the motion that we had drafted on the 25th of November and, indeed, identified the intention for the application to be made in the scheduling order dated the 8th of December. There was likewise an intention also to amend the appellant's brief. It was against that background that I considered the document most likely to assist the Court would be an entirely fresh document that could replace the existing grounds of appeal against the conviction rather than having one document, most of which I was going to abandon anyway, but filleting out really just two parts of it that I wanted to rely on, and then making application in relation to the one fresh ground, which is the new, if leave be granted, ground 2. Such a document would have the advantage of identifying with clarity the issues raised by the appellant and would provide a much easier place of reference for all the parties, and it was against that background that I settled, I hope in an intention to assist, a document entitled "Amended Notice of Appeal" which was filed in accordance with the scheduling order on the 8th of January of this year. That document reduced the grounds of appeal to three, abandoned a number of substantive grounds relied upon hitherto by the Defence and added one entirely new ground, namely ground 2, while seeking to focus the other grounds more on the issues that we would be seeking to raise rather than have them expressed in the all-embracing language that was originally implied. I was, frankly, mortified to receive the Prosecutor's response filed on the 19th of January in which it was thought that I had shown discourtesy to this Court in not indicating in that document, which I had entitled "Amended Notice of Appeal," a paragraph indicating that leave would be sought today to make oral argument in support of that application. I had erroneously thought that having indicated to the Court, as we had, in the motion dated the 25th of November and the terms of the scheduling order of the 8th of December, I thought the combination of those had made it clear that we were today making oral application to amend the notice of appeal, and I had intended that the appellant's brief identified the grounds upon which such application should be made. It would clearly, having seen the Prosecutor's response, have been better to have spelt that out in terms by way of a preliminary paragraph in the notice of appeal, amended notice of appeal, itself, and the fact that I did not do so was not, I can assure the Court, intended as any act of discourtesy against the Tribunal or the Court nor was it intended to inconvenience or be discourteous towards the Prosecution. It may, I'm afraid, reflect a slight unfamiliarity, insofar as I am concerned, with the rules and procedure of this court. For the avoidance of doubt, I am seeking today leave to make oral application to amend the notice of appeal, and I am going to seek to rely upon the submissions contained within the amended appellant's brief to support that application. The error that I have made in not incorporating into the amended notice of appeal an indication that we will be making oral argument today is not, in my submission, an error or omission that ought to be fatal to this process. The Prosecution submits, as I understand it, that irrespective of the merits of the application, the application for leave to amend ought not to be entertained by this Court because of the failure to include in the papers drafted by the 8th of January a specific assertion that they were being drafted as an application for leave to amend. We would invite the Court to treat the documents filed as a de facto application for leave to amend and to treat the application today on its merits, and if the merits and justice require the notice of appeal to be amended, then having heard further argument, to proceed with that amendment; and if the merits and justice do not so require, then, of course, rule accordingly. In our submission, the following points ought to influence the Court in determining whether or not the documents filed should be treated as a de facto application. First -- perhaps, if I may add just before I deal with the point, we would invite the Court in any event to permit me today to make oral application for leave to amend, as was envisaged in the scheduling order of the 8th of December last, and in deciding whether to exercise this Court's discretion and to permit me to make that application, we would rely upon the following points: First, the Prosecution does not suggest that they have been disadvantaged in any way by the lack of clarity in the documents filed and, indeed, that they recognise the intention of the appellant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, may I seek to abbreviate the proceedings by inquiring from the Prosecution whether they are pressing the point that you have not made an application for leave to amend and you are seeking today to have your amended notice of appeal treated as a de facto application for leave to amend. Are you pressing that point, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are pressing the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I am pressing the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: The first fact we rely upon is that the Prosecutor does not suggest that they have been disadvantaged in any way by the lack of clarity in the documents filed and indeed they have recognised the intention of the appellant to seek leave to amend today. They do that in paragraph 37 of their response. Secondly, the failure to draft the documents filed in appropriate terms will not and has not caused any delay because the Prosecutor felt able to respond to the merits of the application, despite their technical failings. Third, to deny the appellant leave to make the application would deny him an opportunity to advance an appeal that may result in his conviction being shown to be unsafe. Four, it would hold the appellant personally at a disadvantage that was a result solely of his lawyer's negligence, and there would seem to be no reason in justice why he should suffer for my drafting inadequacies. Five, it is submitted that it would be an unfortunate result for justice for an appeal, that would otherwise have merit, to be dismissed on a technical ground. Finally, in every jurisdiction of which I am aware, the Court has a discretion to permit an amendment of pleadings during the course of a case, subject to there being no unfairness to the other side. Here, no unfairness is suggested, and we would invite the Court to exercise the discretion that it has in such a way as to permit me today to make an application to amend the grounds of appeal and for the Court to rule upon that application on its merits and not have the application defeated by a pleading technicality. So I don't wish to say anything else in relation to that first discrete issue, unless I can assist the Court any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then will you kindly resume your seat. Mr. Prosecutor, would it be convenient for you to reply, at this stage, to the remarks made by Mr. Clegg on the preliminary issue, if I may so describe it?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I will make my reply. May it please Your Honours. With Your Honours' permission, may I, at the very commencement, make an introductory remark or an introduction of myself because this is the first occasion that I have the privilege of appearing before Your Honours. My background is -- I'm from Sri Lanka, from the Sri Lanka bar. I have had a considerable number of years practising the criminal law. One element I wish to mention, Your Honours, is that Brenda Hollis, the senior trial attorney, is not present before Your Honours today. She has taken ill last evening, and she has not been able to come today. Your Honours, my learned friend, in making submissions, submitted to Your Honours that it was an error on his part in drafting the papers and for having presented the papers in this manner. It was also sought to say that it was an error in understanding the Rules of Procedure of Your Honours' court. If Your Honours please, the Rules of Procedure are meant to keep the decorum and the dignity of Your Honours' court. Counsel, parties appearing before Your Honours, are expected to keep to the Rules so that there will be order before Your Honours' court, and also the Rules seek to see that justice is done, to prevent the miscarriage of justice. We have taken at this point an objection by way of a preliminary objection, Your Honour. The President was pleased to refer to the matter and invite my learned friend to make submissions on the matter, but I must say, with great respect, that he has not understood our objection. He has not made a satisfactory reply to the objection that we have taken. May I, with Your Honours' permission, refer to the motion that was filed by the accused appellant on the 7th of December. On the 7th of December, the motion that was filed by the accused appellant was titled "Motion to Vary the Scheduling Order of 25 November, 1998 and to Adjourn Status Conference of 9 December, 1998." Your Honours were pleased to consider that motion, and Your Honours made the order on the 8th of December. This was referred to by Your Honour, the President. Very clearly, it was stated in very clear terms that the closed session Status Conference to be held on the 9th of December was cancelled. "The appellant shall file any application for leave to amend the notice of appeal." That is the order of Your Honours. "... shall file any application for leave to amend the notice of appeal and the appellant's brief by Friday, 8 January, 1999." So there is no confusion -- there is no reason for there to be any misunderstanding about that order. Thereafter, Your Honours made the order that the Prosecution shall file its response thereto by Monday, 18 January, 1999. Fourthly, the oral argument on such application, oral argument on such application for leave to amend shall, if needed -- if needed, I stress these words, Your Honours, because I strongly believe that Your Honours do consider the preservation of the decorum, the dignity of Your Honours' court, by the obedience to the rules of court will always be respected. "Oral argument on such application for leave to amend shall, if needed, be heard on Monday, 25th January, 1999 commencing at 10.00 a.m. to be followed by a closed session Status Conference." Now, that is the position. So what we say is we are not intending, in any way, to deprive the accused appellant of his rights to place his case. We are not considering the merits of the material that has been submitted by the accused appellant by way of some papers that have been filed before Your Honours. They are not applications. They are not titled as applications, not titled as motions. We just call them papers that have been filed before Your Honours. What was necessary was to title those applications as applications -- those papers as applications before Your Honours. There are no applications before Your Honours. So what we say, with the greatest of respect, my submission is that Your Honours consider that these papers are irrelevant to the present proceedings, irrelevant to the present proceedings. The accused is not deprived of his right to urge his grounds of appeal. The situation would then be that the Court reconsider that there is no application before Your Honours, that there is no application before Your Honours, to amend the notice of appeal, to amend the notice. That was the requirement. If that is so, it is my respectful submission that Your Honours will consider that the case goes back to the situation prior to the 7th of December, in which event I urge Your Honours to make an order in respect of the hearing of the appeal, hearing of the appeal, for the dates to be fixed for the hearing of the appeal. I also respectfully submit that Your Honours be pleased to decide on this issue before proceeding further. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, would you give some further assistance to the bench? In some jurisdictions, there is express legislative authority of one kind or another for a Court of Appeal to grant leave to amend a notice of appeal or the grounds of appeal therein stated. Am I right that there is no corresponding provision in our statutory and regulatory regime? For example, in the United Kingdom, you have the Criminal Appeal Rules of 1968, Rule 2, paragraph 2, subparagraph C, which expressly confers such a power on the Court of Appeal, and no doubt there are similar provisions in other jurisdictions. Now, we do not seem to have such a provision. What is your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, it has been mindful of that position that Your Honours made that order on the 8th of December because there is permission, universally, I should say, permission being granted to amend the notice of appeal. It is in compliance or in accordance with such rule, the universal rule, that Your Honours granted that permission on the 8th of December. Today, the position is that there is no such application before Your Honours. Your Honours suggested de facto -- whether my learned friend would argue on the basis that although it has not been termed an application, whether he would take it as a de facto application before Your Honours. I would, with the greatest of respect, submit that the rules should be strictly adhered to, should be implemented by Your Honours' court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me suggest a point at the other end of the swing of the pendulum. Could there be argument that the absence of a statutory provision empowering the Court to grant leave to amend the grounds of appeal does not denude the Court of the competence which it would have from the normal principle that, in the event of silence, the Court may regulate its own procedure? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With respect, yes. It may be adhering to the normal principles, maybe the inherent powers of Your Honours' court in the interests of justice that permission be granted to amend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: "Inherent" is, perhaps, far too fashionable a word in legal discourse these days. I prefer to speak of a principle which applies. Would you say that in pursuance of that principle, that, in the event of silence, a court, this Court, has competence to regulate its own procedure, the Court may do two things: It may grant leave to amend grounds of appeal, and it may treat some particular documentation as de facto intended to amount to an application for leave to amend? May the Court take that view?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do not intend to stand in the way of an order or ruling by the Court in that way, but my submission is, essentially what has to be considered is by depriving or by rejection or by not accepting these papers before your Court, will the accused be deprived of justice or what he is seeking for? Will there be a miscarriage of justice? It would be my submission that on the papers that have already been filed over a long period of time, over a long period of time, with the greatest of respect, the accused is not deprived of the right to present his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So your position is not that the Court lacks the competence to accede to the motion by the counsel for appellant that the Court should treat the documents filed on the 8th of January as intended to be an application for leave to appeal, you accept the Court has that competence. Your position is the Court should not exercise that competence because appropriate grounds for exercising that in favour of the appellant are absent; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect, yes. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Court will consider this first point before moving on. The Court rules that the appellant may proceed on the basis that his documents of 8th January, 1999 are treated by the Court as intended to be by way of an application for leave to amend. Mr. Clegg, you may, therefore, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Can I move then to deal very briefly with the first ground in that document? It does no more than embrace the original first ground of the appeal settled so long ago but is expressed, I hope, in a rather more focused way, and I thought it helpful to everyone to have one new document that includes that which I intend to argue before this Chamber and excluding that which I do not intend to argue. In one sense, that first ground does not require any application to amend, the Prosecution themselves acknowledge that it's embraced by the original document, but I've included it because I think, hopefully in due course, it will be helpful to have one document that includes all the points, and there are only three of them, that we wish to argue on behalf of this appellant. Insofar as the appellant's brief is concerned so far as this ground is concerned, there was some very trenchant criticism of the original appellant's brief filed by the Prosecution who said, in terms, that it violated an earlier scheduling order made as long ago as the 24th of November, 1997 and was defective in both form and substance. Having read the original appellant's brief, I had considerable sympathy with the response by the Prosecutor to it, and it was against that background that I chose to replace that appellant's brief, which originally amounted to some 237 pages, by a document that certainly embraces the Court's desire for brevity in that it amounts to, I think, ten and, I hope, encapsulates briefly the points that we wish to make on his behalf. It seemed to be sensible to have one document identifying that which we want to argue and to dispose of over 90 per cent of the document that was, in fact, I think, the subject of perfectly legitimate and well-founded criticism. I say no more in relation to that first ground of appeal. That is really only by way of explanation to the Court as to how I approached it. I move now to consider ground 2, and it is that ground that is entirely dependent upon an application under Rule 115. If that application does not find favour with the Court, then the ground is incapable of being sustained. It is this ground that I perhaps slightly prematurely indicated earlier today raises matters so far as evidence is concerned that perhaps ought to be best discussed in closed session. So I would apply that the Chamber now move into closed session to consider my application to amend the grounds of appeal by adding ground 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then it is so ordered. There shall be a closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber has discussed this matter. It is grateful for the assistance it has received from both sides and has reached the following decision nem con. One is that the Chamber grants leave to the appellant to amend his grounds of appeal by the inclusion of grounds 1 and 3 as stated in the amended notice of appeal. The Appeals Chamber refuses leave to amend the grounds of appeal by the inclusion of ground 2 as set out in the amended notice of appeal. The Appeals Chamber rejects the application for leave to admit additional evidence, both as regards ground 2 and ground 3. On the basis that the Prosecution would already have had an opportunity to respond to grounds 1 and 3, the Appeals Chamber refuses further time to the Prosecution for the purpose of responding to those grounds. That ends the consideration of the matters before the Appeals Chamber this morning. The Chamber will now regard the matter as ripe for hearing, and subject to any interventions you have, we will proceed immediately to the holding of a Status Conference to consider the preparation necessary for the hearing of the appeal on the merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? I'm sorry. But in your rulings, I don't see any mention of the appellant's leave to amend the brief of argument as well as the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. The leave granted extends both to the notice of appeal and to the appellant's brief. Thank you for giving me that opportunity to clarify that aspect of the matter. Yes, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Could I just, for the avoidance of doubt, indicate that reliance is, of course, still placed upon the notice of appeal against sentence that was filed on the 14th of July, 1997. It's a wholly separate motion which I think Mr. Keegan accepts and acknowledges. It relates solely to sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that that appeal is affected by anything we have discussed this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Or would you like me to make it clear that nothing discussed this morning or decided this morning affects that appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: adjourned thereafter to be followed by a Status Conference 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
